blurb: Dr. K hosts: FinBERT (Araci 2019) — a transformer that read enough finance text to know “fell sharply” is not a compliment. What a softmax is, why 0.62 is a weak kind of confident, and why even a good reader can't tell you whether a paragraph matters.
intro: Dr. K here, with FinBERT — a transformer that read enough finance text to know that “fell sharply” is not a compliment. This episode, you learn what a softmax is, why 0.62 is a weak kind of confident, and why even a good reader still can't tell you whether a paragraph matters.

body: FinBERT (Araci, 2019) — “FinBERT: Financial Sentiment Analysis with Pre-trained Language Models”, arXiv:1908.10063 — starts from BERT and keeps training it on finance text (a Reuters TRC2 financial subset), then fine-tunes it for sentiment on the Financial PhraseBank (Malo et al., 2014): 4,845 sentences of financial news, labelled by annotators. Note the venue: this is an arXiv preprint and MSc thesis from the University of Amsterdam, not a peer-reviewed journal paper — and it still became the standard finance sentiment model.

Unlike a dictionary, FinBERT reads the whole sentence at once: word order, negation, and context all shape its judgment. That is its strength — semantic context — and its cost: lower direct traceability. You can see its probabilities, but you cannot point at the single word that caused them the way you can with LM.

What it returns is a probability distribution over three classes — positive, negative, neutral — via a softmax. The predicted class is the argmax (the class with the highest probability), and the confidence is the max probability (how high that highest number is).
lessons.h: FinBERT: a transformer that read finance
lessons.tip: LM asks “which list words are here?” FinBERT asks “what does this sentence mean?” Both questions are worth asking — and they can give different answers, which is where Episode 4 begins.

body: Take the sentence: “Revenue fell sharply as costs rose and demand weakened.” Suppose FinBERT returns these probabilities — illustrative teaching values, not a real model run: P(Negative) = 0.62, P(Neutral) = 0.30, P(Positive) = 0.08.
First, check the distribution sums to one: 0.62 + 0.30 + 0.08 = 1.00. A softmax always sums to 1 — if your three numbers don't, something is wrong before you start.
Predicted class = argmax = Negative, because 0.62 is the largest of the three. Confidence = max probability = 0.62.

And 0.62 is a weak kind of confident. ADAM's review threshold is 0.80 — any paragraph whose confidence is below 0.80 goes to a human for review. This paragraph, at 0.62, routes to review, even though its predicted class is clear. A confident-sounding label and a low confidence number can live in the same output.
lessons.h: The worked example, step by step
lessons.tip: Play with the bars below: push Negative to 0.95 and watch the verdict flip to “automated”. Then drag it back to 0.62 and watch it fall into review. The threshold is doing the work, not the label.

body: FinBERT's strength is semantic context: it reads “not expected to face a loss” as reassurance, not as a loss. On the worked example it correctly leans Negative where a dictionary would merely count words. In ADAM's preliminary results it beats the LM dictionary clearly on sentiment (60.7% accuracy vs 37.3% — preliminary, validation ongoing).

Its limits are just as clear. Lower direct traceability: you get probabilities, not a word-by-word receipt. And no disclosure context on its own: FinBERT cannot tell you whether the language is new or carried over from last year, common across the sector or specific to this firm, specific or boilerplate. It answers “what is the tone?” — it does not answer “how informative is this language here and now?”
That is the honest boundary of a sentiment model, however good it is. To cross it you need temporal and peer context — and something to coordinate the evidence. That something is Episode 4.

lessons.h: What FinBERT can and cannot do
lessons.tip: Never ask a sentiment model a question it was not built to answer. “Is this paragraph new?” is not a sentiment question — and FinBERT will happily give you a sentiment answer anyway.

outro: FinBERT reads context beautifully — and still can't tell you if the language is new, boilerplate, or firm-specific. That's a different question, and it needs a different machine. Next: ADAM, where LM and FinBERT stop arguing and start presenting evidence.

quiz.q: FinBERT returns P(Negative) = 0.62, P(Neutral) = 0.30, P(Positive) = 0.08. What is the predicted class and the confidence?
quiz.why: Predicted class = argmax = Negative (0.62 is the largest of the three); confidence = max probability = 0.62. The three probabilities sum to 1.00, but the confidence is the largest single value, not the sum. In short: Negative, confidence 0.62.

quiz.q: What is FinBERT's main strength over the LM dictionary — and its main limit?
quiz.why: FinBERT's strength is semantic context: it reads the whole sentence — word order, negation, context — which LM cannot do. But you get probabilities rather than a word-by-word receipt, and FinBERT alone cannot tell you if language is new, peer-common, or boilerplate. That context question is what ADAM's Context & Quality Agent answers.
